newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices stagger lower again in supply overhang.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices stagger lower again in supply overhang.

text.p: World oil prices staggered lower again on Tuesday as evidence grew that crude markets are becoming increasingly oversupplied in the gap between the seasons for heating oil and gasoline.
London futures for bellwether North Sea Brent Blend were down 22 cents at $19.06 a barrel.

Dealers said that key Atlantic Basin spot markets were suffering a glut of unsold North Sea and west African crude cargoes. Spot price differentials for a range of crude grades were on the slide on Tuesday as buyers took their pick from a raft of shipments.
The U.S. Gulf crude market, the world's biggest import site, was awash with oil, leaving Latin American producers to slash asking prices.
"I think the perception of the market is that we have ample crude," said Nauman Barakat at Prudential Bache in New York.
"I don't think we're going to seen any recovery given the state of the physical market," said a broker in London.
"The gasoline market looks very anaemic also. It should be giving the complex more support at this point. And the heating oil season looks like it's over," Barakat said.
Traders said a heavier than normal schedule of refinery maintenance in the United States and Europe had cut refineries crude requirements.
Last year many refiners postponed maintenance work to keep plants running at full steam to supply demand for heating oil in a northern hemisphere winter which ran into April.
But this year has proved much milder, allowing refiners to rebuild stocks and make leisurely preparations to maximise gasoline for the summer driving season.
Dealers pointed to a deepening contango on the U.S. crude market, pricing prompt oil below crude for delivery further forward, as further evidence of a weak market.
"The oil market in contango is a bearish sign and probably means there's more room on the downside," said Barakat.
Latest monthly oil inventory figures for the European Union, released on Tuesday, only served to undermine markets by revealing large builds in most oil products.
High refinery output and mild weather combined to send EU product inventories up 5.5 million barrels with heating oil now more than 10 percent higher than a year ago, Euroilstock said.
"I really can't see much good news for the market with product levels like these," said Peter Bogin at consultants Cambridge Energy Research Associates.
Weekly U.S. oil inventory data to be published after markets close on Tuesday was also not expected to provide much help.
American Petroleum Institute figures were expected to show a sizeable build in U.S. crude oil stocks, traders said.
